title: Johns Hopkins Study: Time-Restricted Eating Brings Modest Weight Loss Without Counting Calories
excerpt: A 12-week feeding trial found adults with obesity and prediabetes lost a median 2.7% of body weight on a 10-hour eating window — nearly identical to the control group — while improving eating habits but not inflammation or appetite hormones.
body:
• 39 adults with obesity and prediabetes followed either a 10-hour or a 16-hour daily eating window for 12 weeks, with all meals provided and calories set to maintain starting weight.
  • The 10-hour group lost a median 2.7% of body weight, compared with 2.5% in the 16-hour group — a modest and nearly identical result.
  • Both groups reported better eating habits: greater dietary restraint, less stress-driven eating and lower susceptibility to hunger.
  • There was no difference between the groups in appetite hormones or inflammation markers, suggesting meal timing alone adds little beyond the diet itself.

Eating all your meals within a 10-hour window can help people with obesity and prediabetes lose weight without counting calories — but the clock alone appears to add little extra benefit beyond a healthy diet itself, a new Johns Hopkins feeding trial finds.

The 12-week randomized study, led by Dr. Daisy Duan, assistant professor of medicine at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, enrolled 39 adults with obesity and prediabetes or diet-controlled type 2 diabetes. Nineteen were assigned to eat within a 10-hour daily window; the other 20 followed a 16-hour usual eating pattern. The paper was published July 27 in the journal Obesity.

A trial designed to isolate timing

What sets this trial apart is control. All meals were prepared and provided by the Johns Hopkins ProHealth Clinical Research Unit and built on an adapted DASH diet, with calories personalized to maintain each participant's starting weight — meaning nobody was intentionally cutting calories. That let the researchers isolate meal timing from the calorie cuts that have muddied earlier fasting research.

"Other studies on time-restricted eating examined it with respect to either intentional or unintentional calorie restriction," Duan said in a Johns Hopkins release. "The new study focused on whether restricted meal timing while ensuring consistent calorie intake would change other obesity-related factors, such as eating behavior, inflammation, and appetite hormones."

Modest, nearly identical weight loss

The headline result is humbling for fasting enthusiasts. The 10-hour group lost a median 2.7% of body weight over 12 weeks; the 16-hour group lost a median 2.5%. Both groups improved on the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire, reporting greater dietary restraint, less stress-driven eating and lower susceptibility to hunger.

"We saw that people who followed a 10-hour time-restricted eating schedule lost weight and positively changed their eating habits without calorie restriction. But we did not identify any unique, body-wide health benefits linked to the dietary strategy beyond that."

— Dr. Daisy Duan, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine

Fasting blood samples told a similar story: no difference between the groups in the appetite hormones ghrelin and leptin, or in the inflammation markers C-reactive protein, cortisol and sRAGE.

Why it matters

Time-restricted eating — eating only within a consistent daily window, a form of intermittent fasting — has surged in popularity partly on the promise that when you eat matters as much as what you eat. Earlier trials tended to shrink calorie intake automatically, making it impossible to tell whether the clock or the calories were doing the work.

This trial suggests the clock is a modest ally at best: the structured window changed eating behavior for the better, but the weight loss itself came from the controlled diet both groups were already eating.

What it means for South Asians

The findings carry particular weight for South Asians, who develop type 2 diabetes at lower body weights than other populations and bear a disproportionate diabetes burden. Intermittent fasting has deep cultural roots in India — from Navratri fasts to ekadashi — but this study is a reminder that timing strategies work best layered on a genuinely healthy diet, not as a substitute for one.

What's next

The authors' next question is whether time-restricted eating could help people keep weight off after other interventions — for example, after treatment with GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide, where weight regain is common. That maintenance question, Duan's team says, is where the eating window may prove most useful.
